sections.html: The identification of Tatia species is not easy. Although a very recent revision of the genus is available, the species concept used there reflects only a few aspects of coloration, so fish of very different coloration are currently lumped under the same species name. The first attempt to identify these fish went wrong, and they were initially listed erroneously as Tatia cf. gyrina.

Tatia dunni was described in 1945 from Colombia. From 1973 to 2008 it was regarded as synonymous with T. intermedia. T. dunni is widely distributed: there are records of the species from Brazil, Ecuador, Colombia and Peru. However, the fish look quite different in distinct populations. The Peruvian fish, collected near Pucallpa and named "padre abad" by the exporter, differ individually in pattern, but all have in common a golden stripe over the back and a bright golden bar before the dorsal fin.

South America: Upper Amazon in Ecuador and Colombia; central Amazon in Brazil; Caquetá River drainage in Colombia. Type locality: Morelia, Río Caquetá drainage, Colombia.

The species is widely distributed and faces no direct threats. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern (IUCN 2023).

As with others of this genus, give them small pipes, and they also seem to like to hide in the crevices of bogwood. They appear to be happier if they can jam themselves in with the use of their pectoral fins.

Community tanks are fine for this species although you may find that they will predate on fry from other species, but apart from that they come well recommended but don't expect to see them too often.

In its native habitat they feed on small invertebrates and crustaceans and in the aquarium they will eat anything given such as frozen bloodworm inserted into their hideaway, catfish tablets, white worm (sparingly) and prawns and shrimp.

They do like their food and you can see them shooting out of their hideouts and swimming in a frenzied manner to try and take all for themselves, especially when fed their favourite food, frozen bloodworm.

Tatia dunni belongs to the larger species of the genus and may grow longer than 12 cm. However, sexual maturity starts at a much smaller size. In museum material, males were found to have the anal fin modified into a copulatory organ from about 7 cm standard length (that is, without the caudal fin). This modification of the male's anal fin is typical of all driftwood catfishes.

Lexicon: Tatia: dedicated to Charles Tate Regan, ichthyologist at the British Museum. dunni: dedication name. gyrina: from the ancient Greek word for "tadpole". intermedia: Latin, meaning "in between"; the characteristics of the species are intermediate between those of two other species.

Description: Dorsal spines (total): 1; dorsal soft rays (total): 4–5; anal soft rays: 9–10; vertebrae: 35. Can be diagnosed by the unique combination of characters: nasal ossified with narrow medial flanges partially sutured to lateral margin of mesethmoid; anal fin rays iii, 6-7; modified anal fin with short tip in mature males; first unbranched anal-fin ray with segments fused, last branched ray normally developed, not reduced; ribs 10; and vertebrae 35.

Colouration: contour of mouth dark, same colour as head; posterior border of nuchal shield usually dark; pectoral-fin spine usually dark brown; body with irregular blotches or stripes; presence of faint stripes or blotches in large specimens; and caudal fin dark with whitish blotches. Some T. dunni from the Peruvian Amazon have a dark brown body and mottled anal fin. Large specimens from the Purus river, in central Amazonia, usually have a completely dark body or a lightly spotted colouration.

Distinguished from Tatia intermedia by having preanal length 70.0–75.0% SL, vs. 65.0–69.4% SL and interorbital distance 54.1–59.4% HL, vs. 60.1–63.6% HL.

Etymology: dunni: In honour of Emmett Reid Dunn (1894-1956), “in appreciation of his studies on Colombian herpetology”.
